title: Pauri 32, meaning: the steps of the ladder
hookLine: if one tongue became a hundred thousand, I would repeat the Name on each; these are the steps to the Lord (Japji 32)
last: IK DOO JEEBHAU — FROM ONE TONGUE.

lines: NOBODY TAKES IT IN ONE LEAP.
THE NEXT STEP, AND THE NEXT.
cards: A long staircase. A stadium, an old tower, a subway exit when the escalator's broken. Nobody takes it in one leap.
You look at the next step, and the next, and somewhere in the middle you stop counting. Pauri 32 has a staircase too, and it starts on a tongue.

teach.h: A NAME REPEATED, ROUND AFTER ROUND.
teach.b: One tongue became two million. Here's what they'd do. Lakh lakh gerraa aakheeah, ek naam jagdees.

With each tongue, round after round, a hundred thousand times, I would say the one Name of the Lord of the world. Gerraa is a round, like one turn of a wheel. Then: et raah pat pavarreeaa, charreeai hoe ikees.
On this path are the steps to the Beloved; climbing them, one becomes one with Him.
Pavarreeaa, steps. Listen closely and you can hear pauri in it, the name every stanza of Japji carries: a stair, a rung of a ladder. The Japji is built out of steps.
But Nanak doesn't let the climb go to anyone's head.

teach.h: EVEN WORMS COPY TALK OF HEAVEN.
teach.b: Sun galaa aakaas kee, keettaa aaee rees: hearing talk of the heavens, even worms want to copy it. It's a sharp picture of borrowed spiritual talk, people who speak of the top without taking the stairs.
And the last line turns everything: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, koorree koorrai tthees.

teach.h: CLIMB, BUT GRACE BRINGS YOU THERE.
teach.b: By grace it is reached; the boasting of the false is false.
Sikh teachers hold the two halves together. The repeating, round after round, is real effort, a real staircase. The arrival is a gift, the glance of grace.

how: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, sometimes counting on the fingers or on a mala; Pauri 32 pictures repetition of the Name as a staircase, with the arrival given by grace.

o: a long walk to a holy place
a boat for crossing a river
steps, like the rungs of a stair

games.q: what's inside Pauri 32 — tap the pairs.
p: a round, a turn of the wheel

s: pauri, the name of each Japji stanza, means a stair or a ladder's rung
and Pauri 32's word for steps, pavarreeaa, echoes it.
Pauri 32 says the top is reached by effort alone
Nanak nadaree paaeeai: by grace it is reached.
in Pauri 32, even worms want to copy talk of the heavens
a sharp picture of borrowed spiritual talk.

games.q: you've repeated the Name round after round, climbing step by step. in Pauri 32, what finally brings you there?
o: the number of rounds you did.
games.why: Nanak nadaree paaeeai: by grace it is reached, and the boasting of the false is false. the climbing still matters.

practice: In simran, Sikhs repeat Waheguru, a name for the Wondrous Lord; if you'd like, say it twenty times, softly, one finger and one step for each, with no race to the top.
If that word isn't yours, count twenty slow breaths instead, each one a step. At twenty, stop climbing, and just stand on that step and rest, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Pavarreeaa, the steps. One Name repeated on a million tongues: these are the steps to the Beloved. The word echoes pauri itself, and arriving is by grace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 32: the steps; it echoes pauri, a stair or rung.

carryVoice: Your line: step by step. You climb, and you don't brag about the top. That's day two hundred seventeen.
